\chapter{Five Words for a Journey}
\label{ch:el-aeropuerto-y-las-vacaciones}
\hlchaptermodality{392}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el aeropuerto, las vacaciones, el destino, el pasajero and agosto, and name five things about a journey.}

Complete ES-C392-agosto: name five things about a journey, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el aeropuerto]{el aeropuerto — a harbour with air for a sea}

\label{lesson:ES-C392-aeropuerto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the supermarket}, then \emph{the euro}. (\emph{El supermercado}; \emph{el euro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el aire — the first half, standing on its own.
  \item el puerto — the second half, standing on its own.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-e-ro-PUER-to}, five beats with the weight on the fourth. The opening \emph{a} and \emph{e} are two clean vowels in a row, each with its own beat; \emph{ue} runs together into a quick \emph{weh}; the single \emph{r} is a light tap; and the \emph{p} carries no puff of breath behind it. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el aeropuerto} — \textquotedblleft{}the airport.\textquotedblright{}

Two pieces, both visible. Greek \textbf{aēr} was air, and it is the \emph{aero-} of \textbf{aerial} and \textbf{aerobic}. Latin \textbf{portus} was a harbour, and it sits inside English \textbf{port} and \textbf{portal} — and, more quietly, inside \textbf{opportunity}, which is \emph{ob portum}, the wind standing toward the harbour. A favourable wind was your opportunity.

So the picture to keep: a harbour is where things arrive out of the sea. An \emph{aeropuerto} is a harbour whose sea is the air.

Now the part worth being careful about, because the easy answer is not available. The word looks exactly like English \emph{airport}, piece for piece, and that resemblance settles nothing at all. Put \emph{air} beside \emph{harbour} in any European language of the 1920s and you get the same two-part word without anybody copying anybody. That is not speculation — it is documented next door: French \textbf{aéroport} is first attested in 1922, and CNRTL derives it inside French, from \emph{aéro-} plus \emph{port}, rather than out of English.

What can be said honestly is this. \emph{Aeropuerto} belongs to a pan-European habit of early-aviation compounding, and whether Spanish took it from English, took it from French, or built it at home is not known. Structural likeness is the one piece of evidence that cannot decide the question, since every hypothesis predicts it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name where a journey begins: \emph{el aeropuerto}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el aeropuerto}
  \item \emph{un aeropuerto grande}
  \item \emph{estamos en el aeropuerto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{aeropuerto}? (Greek \emph{aēr}, air, and Latin \emph{portus}, a harbour.) And does the word's shape prove Spanish copied English \emph{airport}? (No — air plus harbour gives that shape in several languages independently, and French built \emph{aéroport} at home in 1922; the route into Spanish is open.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[las vacaciones]{las vacaciones — weeks with the duty taken out}

\label{lesson:ES-C392-vacaciones}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the airport}, then \emph{the euro}. (\emph{El aeropuerto}; \emph{el euro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el viaje — what you take during them.
  \item la semana — how they get counted.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{va-ca-CIO-nes}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{v} is a soft \emph{b}, the same sound the letter \emph{b} would give. The \emph{ci} is an \emph{s} across the Americas and a \emph{th} across much of Spain, and \emph{io} runs together into a single beat. The final \emph{s} stays clear and hissed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{las vacaciones} — \textquotedblleft{}the holidays, the vacation.\textquotedblright{} Spanish says it in the plural. The singular \emph{vacación} survives mainly in old talk about an office standing empty.

Latin \textbf{vacāre} was to be empty, to stand free of an obligation. Out of it came \textbf{vacātiō}: exemption, release from a duty. English carries that root several times over — \textbf{vacant}, \textbf{vacate}, \textbf{vacuum}, \textbf{evacuate}, and \textbf{vacation} itself.

The step from \emph{emptiness} to \emph{August by the sea} looks like a leap, and it is not a guessed one. The mid-fifteenth-century English sense of \emph{vacation} was a formal suspension of activity, as of schools and law courts. An empty term. An empty docket. Then, later, empty weeks belonging to you.

This word came into Spanish through a book rather than through a mouth, and it left two fingerprints. The \emph{c} between the vowels is still there, unworn. And the Latin ending arrived as \textbf{-ción}. Compare the same ending after centuries of speech: Latin \emph{ratiōnem} came out as \textbf{razón}. One ending, two roads — \emph{razón} walked, \emph{vacaciones} was carried.

One trap, and it is the likeliest one in this chapter. \textbf{Vaca}, the cow, has nothing to do with any of this. That word is Latin \textbf{vacca}, with a doubled \emph{c}, and the resemblance to the \emph{vac-} of \emph{vacaciones} is pure accident. Cows are not empty; they are unrelated.

\begin{quote}
\emph{estar de vacaciones} — to be away on holiday.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the weeks you leave for: \emph{las vacaciones}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{las vacaciones}
  \item \emph{estoy de vacaciones}
  \item \emph{en el aeropuerto, de vacaciones}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{vacāre} mean? (To be empty, to stand free of a duty.) And is \emph{vacaciones} a relative of \emph{vaca}, the cow? (No — the cow is Latin \emph{vacca}, and the likeness is an accident.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el destino]{el destino — one word doing three jobs}

\label{lesson:ES-C392-destino}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the airport}, then \emph{the holidays}. (\emph{El aeropuerto}; \emph{las vacaciones}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item estar — the standing verb from the same Latin root.
  \item la ciudad — one thing a \emph{destino} can be.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{des-TI-no}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{i} is the \emph{ee} of \emph{see}, never the \emph{i} of \emph{sit}. The \emph{t} is dental, tongue on the back of the teeth and no puff after it. Note too that \emph{st} sits happily inside the word, where a Spanish word opening on those two letters puts an \emph{e} in front first: \emph{estar}, \emph{estudiante}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el destino} — the destination. And two more things besides.

Latin \textbf{dēstināre} was \emph{dē-} plus an element belonging to \textbf{stāre}, to stand: to make firm, to fix a thing in place. Spanish took the verb \textbf{destinar} straight off the written page, and the dates say so plainly. Corominas finds \emph{destinar} no earlier than the fifteenth century, and \emph{destino} first in Garcilaso, between 1503 and 1536. A word surfacing that late has not been rubbing along in people's mouths since Rome; it was read into the language.

English got the same Latin: \textbf{destiny}, \textbf{destination}, \textbf{destine}, and the lovely \textbf{obstinate}, someone standing firmly in the way. Further back still, plain \textbf{stand} and \textbf{stable} are cousins.

Here is the most useful thing in the lesson, and it is a false friend three ways over. English \emph{destination} means one thing. Spanish \emph{destino} means three:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{fate} — \emph{el destino quiso otra cosa}, fate wanted something else;
  \item \textbf{the end of a journey} — \emph{nuestro destino es Madrid};
  \item \textbf{a job posting}, a duty station, which the Academy glosses with the single word \emph{empleo} — \emph{un destino en el extranjero} is work abroad, not a holiday.
\end{itemize}

So when you hear \emph{su destino es la capital}, the sentence has two readings, and only context tells you whether the person is flying there or has been assigned there. Fixing a plane's endpoint and fixing an officer's post are the same act of \emph{dēstināre}: putting something firmly where it will be.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name where the journey ends: \emph{el destino}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el destino}
  \item \emph{nuestro destino}
  \item \emph{un destino de vacaciones}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{dēstināre} mean? (To make firm, to fix a thing in place.) And name the third sense of \emph{destino}, the one English \emph{destination} has no room for. (A job posting or duty station — the Academy's \emph{empleo}. Fate is the other.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pasajero]{el pasajero — an adjective that was given a seat}

\label{lesson:ES-C392-pasajero}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the holidays}, then \emph{the destination}. (\emph{Las vacaciones}; \emph{el destino}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pasaporte — the same \emph{pasar}, at the gate.
  \item billete — what this person is holding.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-sa-JE-ro}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{j} is a rough throat sound, further back than English \emph{h}. The single \emph{r} between vowels is a light tap rather than a roll, and both \emph{s} stay clear and hissed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pasajero} — \textquotedblleft{}the passenger.\textquotedblright{} Built in three moves, each one visible.

\textbf{Pasar}, to pass, goes back through Vulgar Latin \textbf{passāre} to Latin \textbf{passus}, a step — the stride of a marching legion. Add \emph{-aje} and you get \textbf{pasaje}, a passing, a crossing, a fare. Add \emph{-ero}, the ending for the person who deals in a thing, and you get \emph{pasajero}: the one making the crossing.

The middle piece has a passport of its own. \textbf{-aje} came in from Old French \textbf{-age} and Occitan \textbf{-atge}, and it lives in Spanish beside its inherited twin \textbf{-azgo}, the ending the language grew at home. So \emph{pasaje} is not a purely native build: Latin stem, borrowed ending, arriving early — Corominas has \emph{pasaje} by 1309 and \emph{pasajero} by Nebrija.

Two traps, and both repay the attention.

The first is what kind of word this is. The Academy's opening sense is not the person at all: \emph{que pasa presto o dura poco} — passing quickly, lasting little. Fleeting. \emph{Un dolor pasajero} is a pain that goes away. Even the traveller senses are filed as that same adjective, doing duty as a noun. A passenger, in Spanish, is a \emph{passing one} who has been made into a person.

The second is a letter. English \textbf{passenger} carries an \emph{n} that was never in the word — \emph{passager} picked it up in the early fifteenth century, in company with \textbf{messenger}, \textbf{harbinger} and \textbf{scavenger}, which all did the same thing. Etymonline's account of why is honest and short: it was done \textquotedblleft{}for no apparent reason except that people liked to say it that way.\textquotedblright{} Spanish never caught the habit. \emph{Pasajero}, never \emph{pasanjero}.

English keeps the rest of the family in \textbf{passage}, \textbf{pass}, \textbf{pace} and \textbf{compass}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name who is travelling: \emph{el pasajero}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pasajero}
  \item \emph{los pasajeros}
  \item \emph{el pasajero y su destino}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Academy's first sense of \emph{pasajero}? (Fleeting, short-lived — an adjective; the passenger is that adjective made into a noun.) And which letter does English \emph{passenger} carry that Spanish never had? (The \emph{n}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[agosto]{agosto — an emperor with a vowel missing}

\label{lesson:ES-C392-agosto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the destination}, then \emph{the passenger}. (\emph{El destino}; \emph{el pasajero}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item los meses — the list this one belongs to.
  \item el calor — what the month brings with it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-GOS-to}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{g} is hard, as in English \emph{go}. The \emph{s} stays clear. The \emph{t} is dental, tongue against the back of the teeth, with no puff of breath after it. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{agosto} — \textquotedblleft{}August.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{Augustus}, the emperor; the month had an older name and was renamed in his honour. This word travelled by mouth, not by book, and it carries the mileage on it in two places.

The first is the stressed vowel. \emph{Augustus} had a \emph{u} there; \emph{agosto} has an \textbf{o} — what a word gets from centuries of being spoken. Set beside it the twin that came the other way: Spanish also has \textbf{augusto}, the adjective, majestic or lofty, lifted straight off the Latin page, and it still has its \emph{au} and its \emph{u}, both untouched. One Latin word, two Spanish descendants: \emph{agosto} out of the mouth, \emph{augusto} out of the book.

The second is a genuine puzzle. The opening \emph{au} should not have come out as \emph{a}. Look at what happened to its neighbours:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Latin \emph{causa} gave Spanish \textbf{cosa};
  \item Latin \emph{taurum} gave Spanish \textbf{toro}.
\end{itemize}

On that showing, \emph{Augustus} ought to have produced \emph{ogosto}. It did not, because Spanish never started from \emph{Augustus}. It started from \textbf{agustus}, a Vulgar Latin form attested from the mid-to-late first century CE, in which the \emph{au} had already given way to \emph{a} under the pull of the \emph{u} in the next syllable. Catalan and Occitan \textbf{agost} point back to that same starting line, and Corominas dates the Spanish word to 1192.

One thing stays open. What the name \emph{Augustus} meant to begin with is disputed — consecrated by the augurs, perhaps; or built on \emph{augeo}, to increase. Two respectable answers, and no settled verdict between them.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words and a journey: \emph{el aeropuerto}, \emph{las vacaciones}, \emph{el destino}, \emph{el pasajero}, \emph{agosto}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Name five things about a journey, and say one thing about each.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el aeropuerto} — \emph{el aeropuerto es grande}
  \item \emph{las vacaciones} — \emph{estoy de vacaciones}
  \item \emph{el destino} — \emph{mi destino es la ciudad}
  \item \emph{el pasajero} — \emph{el pasajero tiene su billete}
  \item \emph{agosto} — \emph{en agosto hace calor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Spanish word kept the \emph{au} and the \emph{u} of \emph{augustus}? (\emph{Augusto}, the adjective — the copy that came off the page.) And why does \emph{agosto} not begin like \emph{cosa} and \emph{toro}? (Because Spanish started from the attested Vulgar Latin \emph{agustus}, whose \emph{au} had already become \emph{a}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
